extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for newsroom language, terminology, capitalization, and usage when reporting about identities, religions, medical conditions, cultures, and related topics to avoid inaccuracy and offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: allahu akbar
rubrics_metrics.description: In Arabic it means “God is great” or “God is the greatest.” Muslims say it several times a day, such as during the call for prayer, during prayer, when they are happy and when they wish to express their approval of what they hear.

rubrics_metrics.name: ally
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who makes the commitment and effort to recognize their privilege (based on gender, class, race, sexual identity, etc.) and work in solidarity with oppressed groups in the struggle for justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allies understand it's in their interest to end oppression; they commit to reducing complicity and strengthening their own knowledge and awareness of oppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alzheimer's disease
rubrics_metrics.description: A progressive and fatal disease in which nerve cells in the brain degenerate and brain matter shrinks, resulting in impaired thinking, behavior and memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the term Alzheimer’s disease (never Alzheimer’s). Disclose an individual has Alzheimer’s disease only if relevant and formally diagnosed by a licensed medical professional. Refer to someone as having Alzheimer’s disease rather than 'suffers from' or 'afflicted with.'

rubrics_metrics.name: America
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers to the entire Western hemisphere and does not apply solely to the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Americas for North and South America together. When referring to the United States, use United States, U.S., U.S.A., or the States.

rubrics_metrics.name: American
rubrics_metrics.description: People who live in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that many in Latin America also see themselves as Americans; some view 'American' as imperialist. Still, American is the most widely recognized term for people who live in the United States of America.

rubrics_metrics.name: American Indian
rubrics_metrics.description: American Indian and Native American are generally acceptable and can be used interchangeably; individuals may have a preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tribal affiliation when reporting on individuals. 'Native American' expanded to include all Native people of the continental U.S. and some in Alaska; the term is used only to describe groups of Native Americans (two or more). Use native-born to describe someone born in the United States but not American Indian. Note: federal government considers someone American Indian if they belong to a federally recognized tribe; tribes determine membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: American Indian Movement
rubrics_metrics.description: Activist organization known as AIM, founded in 1968 to promote civil rights for Native Americans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Founded to seek recognition of treaty rights through sit-ins and protests; notable action: 1972 'Trail of Broken Treaties.' AIM has branches across the United States.

rubrics_metrics.name: American Indian or Alaska Native, U.S. Census definition of
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. Census Bureau defines American Indian or Alaska Native as a person having origins in any of the original peoples of North and South America (including Central America) and who maintains tribal affiliation or community attachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Census racial categories reflect social definitions, not biological or anthropological definitions; categories include national origin or sociocultural groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: American Sign Language
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete language that utilizes signs made by moving the hands combined with facial expressions and postures of the body; many deaf or hard of hearing in North America use it as a primary means of communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify American Sign Language on first reference, capitalizing all three words. ASL is acceptable on second reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal civil rights legislation created in 1990 to address discrimination on the basis of disability in employment, public accommodations, transportation and telecommunications, and government services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Americans with Disabilities Act on first reference; ADA is acceptable on second reference. For more info, visit ADA.gov.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amish
rubrics_metrics.description: Descendants of Swiss Anabaptists known for plain clothes and rejecting some modern technology; base morals on the Bible and unwritten rules called the Ordnung.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amish pastors are called bishops.

rubrics_metrics.name: amputation, amputee
rubrics_metrics.description: Amputation refers to removal of a bodily extremity, usually during surgery. Amputee is the acceptable term for someone who has undergone an amputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Someone with an amputation or an amputee are both acceptable. Note some people have physical deformities not resulting from amputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: anchor baby, anchor child
rubrics_metrics.description: A child born to a non-citizen mother in a country that grants automatic citizenship to children born on its soil, especially if parents plan the birth to secure citizenship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term is pejorative; avoid except in quotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: androgyne
rubrics_metrics.description: A person whose biological sex is not readily apparent or who is between two genders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best to ask which pronouns they prefer. See agender, genderqueer, non-binary gender.

rubrics_metrics.name: androphilic, gynephilic
rubrics_metrics.description: Attraction to males/masculinity (andro) or to females/femininity (gyne).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative terms to avoid gendering the person while expressing attraction to a particular gender; used in place of homosexual/heterosexual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angel Island
rubrics_metrics.description: West Coast counterpart to Ellis Island; from 1910–1940 the U.S. Immigration Station processed many immigrants, majority from China; held POWs during WWII.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Angel Island is now a state park run by California Dept. of Parks and Recreation; virtual tour available from the Angel Island Immigration Station Foundation.

rubrics_metrics.name: annul, annulment
rubrics_metrics.description: In Catholic Church, an annulment (declaration of nullity) means the sacramental bond of matrimony never existed because a party was unwilling or unable to make and keep sacramental promises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A declaration that the sacrament did not exist does not mean a loving marriage relationship never existed and does not make children illegitimate in church or civil law.

rubrics_metrics.name: antisemitism
rubrics_metrics.description: Prejudice against people of Jewish heritage; has inspired the Holocaust and other crimes. Religious antisemitism blames Jews for killing Jesus (deicide); economic/political antisemitism refers to conspiratorial claims about Jewish power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spelling debate exists; many organizations favor unhyphenated 'antisemitism' in early 2020s. See IHRA, Jewish Virtual Library, ADL for more on spelling and usage. Updated November 2023.

rubrics_metrics.name: apartheid
rubrics_metrics.description: Racial segregation and political/economic discrimination enforced by white minority government against non-white residents in South Africa from 1948 to 1994.

rubrics_metrics.name: apocalypse, apocalyptic
rubrics_metrics.description: A final cosmic battle between good and evil that encompasses Earth; for believers it ushers in God's reign and the righteous being raised to everlasting life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lowercase 'apocalypse' when referring to the battle ending the world; uppercase when using the traditional Catholic name for the Book of Revelation. Catholic News Service advises using 'Revelation' instead of 'Apocalypse' except in direct quotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arab
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers to a nation or people from an Arabic-speaking country; not synonymous with Muslim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When referring to events in a specific country, name the country rather than generalizing 'Arab.' Use Arab as noun or adjective. Do not imply Arab equals Muslim, holy war, or terrorist. Note Iran is not an Arab country; most Iranians are Persian and speak Farsi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arab American, American Arab
rubrics_metrics.description: A U.S. citizen or permanent resident who traces ancestry to, or immigrated from, Arabic-speaking places in the Middle East and North Africa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all people in the region are Arabs. 'Arab American' is preferred over 'American Arab.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Arab League
rubrics_metrics.description: The League of Arab States, an umbrella organization with 22 members across North Africa, the Horn of Africa, and Southwest Asia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes list of member countries and admittance years; when reporting, use formal name 'League of Arab States' where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arabian
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjective referring to Saudi Arabia, the Arabian Peninsula, or things associated (e.g., Arabian horse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ethnicity or nationality is relevant, be more precise by specifying the country (Lebanese, Yemeni, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arabic
rubrics_metrics.description: Name of the language spoken in Arab countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally not used as an adjective (guidance: prefer 'Arab' as adjective for people/things?).

rubrics_metrics.name: argilah, argeelah
rubrics_metrics.description: A water pipe that filters and cools tobacco smoke; smoke usually flavored and known by names including sheesha and hookah.

rubrics_metrics.name: aromantic
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who does not experience romantic attraction; may or may not be asexual and may still feel other forms of attraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See asexual.

rubrics_metrics.name: articulate
rubrics_metrics.description: Calling a Black person 'articulate' can imply surprise and be insulting or imply they 'talk white.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using 'articulate' to describe Black people because it can carry negative implications and authenticity judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aryan
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally from Sanskrit 'arya' meaning 'noble' in scholarly usage; term was appropriated in late 19th century into anti-Semitic ideology and neo-Nazi usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In modern white supremacist usage, refers to non-Jewish white people, especially of Scandinavian heritage.

rubrics_metrics.name: asexual
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who does not experience sexual attraction; may experience other forms of attraction and intimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ash Wednesday
rubrics_metrics.description: The Wednesday marking the beginning of Lent in Western Christian churches, involving putting ashes on foreheads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common among Roman Catholics, Anglicans, Episcopalians, many Lutherans, and increasingly other Protestant churches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ashkenazi
rubrics_metrics.description: A Jew of German, Polish, Austrian, or Eastern European descent; historically spoke Yiddish and constituted majority of Jews in the U.S.; referred to as Ashkenazim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pronunciation: 'osh-ken-AH-zee.' See Sephardi for contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asia
rubrics_metrics.description: Home to about 60% of world's population; traditional regional breakdowns: East Asia, South Asia, Southeast Asia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In American usage, 'Asian' often refers to entire continent but can be shorthand for East Asians; British usage often refers to South Asians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asia, Central
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution — term is vague; may include Mongolia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan; historical definitions vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise country names when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asia, use and abuse of images from
rubrics_metrics.description: Cautions against stereotypical imagery (Taj Mahal, Ganges, Great Wall, pagodas, cheongsam, rice paddies, rickshaws, samurais, geishas, etc.) when representing Asia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When used in context, such images can be appropriate; when altered or used to stereotype or caricature, they can be problematic. Avoid exoticizing or stereotyping through inappropriate imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asian
rubrics_metrics.description: A broad term; in some British usage refers to South Asians; in U.S. usage often used for East Asians or entire continent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise caution; be specific (e.g., Chinese, Japanese, South Asian) when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asian American
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper term for people who come from Asia or descend from people who lived in Asia; do not hyphenate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, ask people how they identify (e.g., Chinese American). 'South Asian' can refer to Indians, Pakistanis, Bangladeshis; use East Asian to refer to Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Vietnamese, etc. Updated February 2021.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asian Exclusion Acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws where Congress barred or sharply restricted immigration of Asians to the U.S., e.g., Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, 1924 Oriental Exclusion Act, 1934 Tydings-McDuffie Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualize historical quotas and repeals; note expansions in immigration policy after 1965.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asian names
rubrics_metrics.description: More complex than European names; clarify family and surname and rules for second reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask subjects about preferred forms and pronunciations. When in doubt, ask. Consider including pronunciation explainers in text, broadcast, or graphics. See Vietnamese names and Southeast Asian names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asian religions
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution: religion is an imprecise term in Asia; practices like temples, meditation, and concepts of Buddha may differ from Judeo-Christian-Islamic concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise; see Buddhism, Confucianism, Hinduism, Islam, Shintoism, Taoism for specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asian, U.S. Census definition of
rubrics_metrics.description: Census defines Asian as a person having origins in any of the original peoples of the Far East, Southeast Asia, or the Indian subcontinent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Census notes racial categories reflect social definitions; Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander refers to peoples of Hawaii, Guam, Samoa, or other Pacific Islands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asiatic
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid — term is a vestige of European colonialism and imperialism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's a 19th-century adjective used in 'scientific' European treatises assuming white superiority; avoid usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: ASL
rubrics_metrics.description: See American Sign Language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asperger's syndrome
rubrics_metrics.description: Formerly a distinct diagnosis, now part of autism spectrum disorder; characterized by social interaction difficulties, restricted interests, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to someone as having Asperger’s syndrome only if relevant and formally diagnosed. Some diagnosed before 2013 prefer the term. Use 'person diagnosed with Asperger’s syndrome' or 'person with Asperger’s syndrome.' 'Syndrome' not capitalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: assisted living facility
rubrics_metrics.description: A housing option for older people who can't live independently and need help with medications and daily activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes referred to as ALFs in the senior living industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: atheist
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who does not believe in God or other supernatural forces; distinctions exist between 'weak' and 'strong' atheism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See agnostic for related terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: attention-deficit disorder (ADD)/attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical community now refers to ADHD with subtypes; symptoms include restlessness, difficulty focusing, impulsivity; ADHD diagnosis more commonly used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to someone as having ADD/ADHD only if relevant and formally diagnosed by a licensed medical professional. Use full term on first reference; ADD/ADHD acceptable on second reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aunt Jemima
rubrics_metrics.description: Nancy Green, born a slave, became advertising trademark as Aunt Jemima; seen by some as painful reminder of slavery and negative stereotype.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualize historical background and potential offensiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: aunt, uncle
rubrics_metrics.description: When not referring to family relationships, terms can be insensitive depending on context; historically used by whites to address black servants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Black communities, terms used as endearment or respect. Traditionally in the South, children address adults with honorifics like Miss, Ma'am, Aunt, Mister, Uncle, Sir.

rubrics_metrics.name: auntie
rubrics_metrics.description: In many cultures a term of respect, not necessarily indicating family relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An Arab American might call an older person 'auntie' ('amty') or 'uncle' ('ammo'). See aunt, uncle.

rubrics_metrics.name: autism/autism spectrum disorders
rubrics_metrics.description: Group of complex disorders related to brain development with variable symptoms including communication difficulties and restricted patterns of behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to someone as having autism spectrum disorder only if relevant and formally diagnosed. Ask individuals how they prefer to be described; if in doubt use people-first language 'person with autism spectrum disorder.' See Asperger’s syndrome.

rubrics_metrics.name: ayatollah
rubrics_metrics.description: A Shiite term for a senior clergyman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize when used as a title before a name, lowercase otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: B.C.
rubrics_metrics.description: Literally, 'before Christ' or the Christian era.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars/textbooks increasingly use B.C.E. and C.E. to avoid Christian-centered dating. See A.D.

rubrics_metrics.name: baby boom
rubrics_metrics.description: A period marked by greatly increased birth rate, commonly used for post-WWII births (Baby Boomer Generation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. Census Bureau estimates 76 million Americans born 1946–1964. See related Census report for more detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bahá’í, the Bahá’í Faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Monotheistic religion teaching progressive revelation; founder Bahá’u’lláh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms Bahaism and Bahaist are incorrect; use 'the Bahá’í Faith' for the religion and 'Bahá’í' for an adherent. For more, go to bahai.org.

rubrics_metrics.name: banana
rubrics_metrics.description: Slang term and pejorative used by Asian Americans to refer to Asian Americans who identify more with whites than other Asian Americans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only in direct quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baptist
rubrics_metrics.description: When capitalized, generally refers to a Protestant group marked by baptism by immersion of individuals who profess faith in Jesus Christ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Baptists commonly call the practice believer’s baptism, distinguishing them from groups practicing infant baptism. Entry modified to remove 'evangelical' and add 'Protestant.'

rubrics_metrics.name: bar mitzvah, bat mitzvah
rubrics_metrics.description: A milestone in Judaism when a person is responsible for their own actions spiritually and ethically; bar for boys at 13, bat for girls at 12.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technically refers to the child coming of age; strict usage is 'becoming a bar/bat mitzvah,' though common usage refers to ceremony as 'having a bar mitzvah.'

rubrics_metrics.name: belonging
rubrics_metrics.description: A sense of fitting in or feeling accepted and valued by a group, workplace, society, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term is used with diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives and committees; sometimes abbreviated DEIB. Added April 2023.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bible Belt
rubrics_metrics.description: Areas of the U.S. noted for prevalence of strict evangelical Christian teachings, particularly in the South and Midwest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be considered offensive in some contexts; use carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bible-believing
rubrics_metrics.description: Term used by some Christians to describe emphasis on Scripture authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using this term except when people use it to describe themselves, because by definition all Christians believe the Bible.

rubrics_metrics.name: bindi, or bindhi
rubrics_metrics.description: Decoration worn on the forehead by many Hindu women; pronounced 'BIN-dhee.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Has various cultural and religious explanations (marriage symbol, third eye, decoration). Worn by Indians of all religions.

rubrics_metrics.name: biological gender/biological sex
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the terms 'biological gender,' 'biological sex,' 'biological woman/man' as inaccurate and often offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When necessary, refer to assigned sex at birth using 'assigned male at birth' or 'assigned female at birth.' Consider whether story requires this information. Updated March 2021.

rubrics_metrics.name: biphobia
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear of bisexuals, often based on stereotypes like promiscuity or infidelity; better described as intolerance or prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See bisexual.

rubrics_metrics.name: BIPOC
rubrics_metrics.description: Acronym for Black, Indigenous, and People of Color, intended to unite people of color while acknowledging different forms of oppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not say 'BIPOC people' (redundant). Pronounced 'buy-pock.' Term rose in prevalence in 2020; not universally embraced by all. See references for background reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: bipolar disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental illness characterized by intense shifts in emotion, energy and behavior in mood episodes (manic, hypomanic, depressive, mixed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to someone as having bipolar disorder only if central to the story and formally diagnosed. Do not use 'bipolar' casually as adjective for rapid changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: biracial, multiracial, mixed-race, two or more races
rubrics_metrics.description: Biracial refers to people of two races; multiracial refers to people of two or more racial backgrounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred terms: multiracial, biracial, multiethnic, polyethnic. Use mixed/mixed-race with caution as some find offensive; others embrace them. Updated February 2021.

rubrics_metrics.name: birth defect
rubrics_metrics.description: See defect/birth defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black Africa
rubrics_metrics.description: See Africa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black church
rubrics_metrics.description: Collective noun referring to the many Christian churches with predominance of Black members and clerical leadership; major institutional foundation in Black community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally refers to Protestants (variety of denominations); doesn't generally encompass Catholics, Muslims, or others. May be more accurate to say 'Black churches' in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black Codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes curtailing the rights of African Americans during early Reconstruction (1865–1866) instituted by Southern legislatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also called Negro Codes; aimed to restore political and economic structure of slavery via restrictions like forbidding Black people from owning or renting farmland.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black diaspora
rubrics_metrics.description: See African diaspora.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black English, African American English
rubrics_metrics.description: See Ebonics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black leader
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using the term 'Black leader' because it implies one person speaks for all Black people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When referring to a local Black person in leadership, state the organization they belong to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black Lives Matter, #BlackLivesMatter
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil rights movement started after 2013 acquittal of George Zimmerman; began as a Twitter hashtag and call to action against anti-Black racism and police violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Movement does not assert Black lives are more important than others; it highlights disproportionate threats faced by Black people and stands with other oppressed peoples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black Muslim
rubrics_metrics.description: Term became associated with the Nation of Islam and is now considered derogatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred term is 'member of the Nation of Islam.' Do not use 'Black Muslim' to describe African-Americans who practice traditional Islam; instead say 'African-American Muslims.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Black or African American, U.S. Census definition of
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. Census Bureau definition (chunk truncated before full definition).
